scenes.anchor: right now if your hearing is normal
scenes.visual: Dark slate. A chalk profile head (the one S05 later opens up). Out of the ear, faint violet rings grow, slow and steady, and never stop. A panel beside it draws the steady violet tone trace. 1 s beat after the first line: only the pulse.
changes: violet rings start at the ear on 'making a sound'
steady tone trace draws on 'faint steady tone'
rings reach further out on 'into your ear canal'
scenes.words: right now if your hearing is normal there's a good chance your ears are making a sound not ringing usually far too quiet to notice a faint steady tone made inside your ear and slipping out into your ear canal it sounds like a myth

scenes.anchor: but play a sound into a healthy ear
scenes.visual: A row of seven chalk newborn cots (simple outlines, no faces) under 'newborn hearing screen'. Match to the chalk probe-in-canal section; chalk click rings travel in; a scope trace waits, flat, as the probe listens.
changes: head and pulse give way to a row of newborn cots on 'hospitals count on it'
cots give way to the probe diagram on 'soft probe'
three chalk click rings travel in on 'quiet clicks'
scope trace appears and sweeps, flat, on 'it listens'
scenes.words: but play a sound into a healthy ear and it answers so reliably that hospitals count on it almost every newborn in america gets a hearing test usually before leaving the hospital in one common version a soft probe plays quiet clicks into the baby's ear and then it listens

scenes.anchor: it's waiting for a sound to come back out
scenes.visual: A violet ring emerges from deep inside the ear (beyond the eardrum) and travels OUT to the probe; the scope trace shows a small violet wiggle a few ms after the click.
changes: violet ring leaves the inner ear on 'made inside'
scope wiggles violet on 'the ear itself'
scenes.words: it's waiting for a sound to come back out not an echo off the eardrum a sound made inside the ear itself

scenes.anchor: healthy ears talk back
scenes.visual: Back to the profile head, centred, violet rings at the ear; the title lands.
scenes.words: healthy ears talk back

scenes.anchor: to see why we have to take apart
scenes.visual: One head stays; the others fade. Ear cross-section draws in chalk over it (outer, middle, inner ear) and becomes the corner locator for the rest of the episode.
changes: shrinks to corner locator at the end
scenes.words: to see why we have to take apart the ear we think we have

scenes.anchor: here's the ear most of us picture
scenes.visual: Full ear section: canal, eardrum, the three ossicles, the coiled cochlea. Chalk sound rings travel down the canal; the eardrum flexes; the bone chain rocks; the stirrup plunges at the oval window.
changes: bones rock in sequence on 'hammer the anvil and the stirrup'
stirrup lights on 'entrance of the cochlea'
scenes.words: here's the ear most of us picture sound travels down the ear canal and makes the eardrum vibrate three tiny bones the hammer the anvil and the stirrup pass that vibration on to the entrance of the cochlea

scenes.anchor: the stirrup the last of the three
scenes.visual: Gray's Anatomy 1918 plate of the ossicle chain, inked chalk-on-slate (inverted), with a 3 mm scale bar drawn beside the stirrup and a grain of rice outline for scale (rice size not stated as fact).
text: STIRRUP · smallest bone in the body
scenes.asset: G1 Gray's Anatomy 1918, fig. 919 chain of ossicles (public domain, archive.org)
scenes.words: the stirrup the last of the three is the smallest bone in the human body about three millimetres long

scenes.anchor: simple enough
scenes.visual: The ear section restyles as a microphone schematic (diaphragm, linkage, transducer) for a beat, then back.
scenes.words: simple enough a microphone with some plumbing

scenes.anchor: but why the bones at all
scenes.visual: Split: air on the left, fluid on the right (muted hatching, never blue: blue means cold). Chalk sound rings hit the boundary; almost all bounce back, a sliver gets through. A counter shows 99.9% reflected.
scenes.words: but why the bones at all why not let the air push on the cochlea directly because the cochlea is full of fluid and when sound in air hits fluid about ninety nine point nine percent of its energy simply bounces off like shouting at someone underwater

scenes.anchor: so the middle ear concentrates the push
scenes.visual: Eardrum as a big disc, stirrup footplate as a tiny one, same force arrow-less push lines converging; then a stiletto heel outline pressing on a floor beside a flat shoe.
changes: big disc vs tiny disc on 'fifteen to twenty times'
lever pivot on the bones on 'leverage'
scenes.words: so the middle ear concentrates the push the eardrum is roughly fifteen to twenty times bigger than the footplate of the stirrup the same force focused onto a tiny spot like a stiletto heel the little bones add a bit of leverage on top together they raise the pressure reaching the cochlea many times over

scenes.anchor: and here's an odd detail
scenes.visual: Drafting card: a reptile-like ancestor skull in profile with its jaw joint highlighted (two small bones), then a time slider runs and those two bones shrink and migrate into the middle ear of a mammal skull. Bird/reptile ear shows one bone.
changes: jaw joint bones highlight on 'jaw joint'
settle in the ear on 'carrying sound'
text: hammer + anvil: once the jaw joint
scenes.words: and here's an odd detail birds and reptiles have just one ear bone the stirrup our other two the hammer and the anvil began as the bones of the jaw joint in our distant reptile like ancestors over many millions of years those old jaw bones shrank and ended up carrying sound instead

scenes.anchor: so far this is all passive
scenes.visual: Back on the ear section; everything gentle. Push in through the oval window toward the cochlea; corner locator boxes the cochlea.
changes: push in on 'what they hand it to'
scenes.words: so far this is all passive bones and levers handing vibration along the surprise is in what they hand it to

scenes.anchor: inside your skull sits the cochlea
scenes.visual: HERO 1 (3D). The cochlea as a matte bone-white snail shell (2.5 turns, ~9 mm base, built to the reference numbers in assets.md), slowly rotating under a cool rim light on slate. Then it UNCOILS: the spiral straightens into a ~3 cm tube, with the basilar membrane strip running along its length, visibly narrow at one end and wide at the other.
scenes.words: inside your skull sits the cochlea a fluid filled tube coiled like a snail shell about two and a half turns unrolled it would be only about three centimetres long running along it is a strip called the basilar membrane and it changes from one end to the other

scenes.anchor: near the entrance the base
scenes.visual: The straight membrane in 2D (match to the hero's last frame): BASE narrow and stiff (tight chalk hatching), APEX wide and floppy (loose hatching).
scenes.words: near the entrance the base it's narrow and stiff at the far end the apex it's wider and much floppier

scenes.anchor: so each spot along it responds most
scenes.visual: Piano keys fade in beneath the membrane, high keys under the base, low keys under the apex. A pitch slider moves and a chalk bump peaks at the matching place.
changes: high note bump near base on 'high notes'
low note bump near apex on 'low notes'
scenes.words: so each spot along it responds most to one pitch high notes near the base low notes near the apex pitch is laid out along the spiral a bit like the keys of a piano from about twenty vibrations a second to about twenty thousand

scenes.anchor: when a sound arrives a ripple runs
scenes.visual: HERO 2 (3D). The straight membrane as a long ribbon; a travelling wave rolls from the base, grows to a peak at one place and dies. Plays twice with two pitches (peak near base, then near apex). Neutral render; the wave crest gets a thin chalk overlay line.
changes: wave starts at base on 'from the base'
scenes.words: when a sound arrives a ripple runs along the membrane from the base grows to a peak at the place tuned to that pitch then quickly dies away a travelling wave

scenes.anchor: the man who showed this was georg von
scenes.visual: Drafting title card (no portrait: none is public domain): name, 1961 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and a small cadaver-cochlea specimen jar line drawing.
scenes.words: the man who showed this was georg von b k sy he won the nineteen sixty one nobel prize for it and he worked it out largely with cochleas from human cadavers that turned out to matter

scenes.anchor: because the dead ears missed something
scenes.visual: Two response curves on one chart: DEAD (broad, low, muted chalk) and LIVING (tall, sharp peak, chalk with a violet core). The living curve collapses to the dead one when a 'death' marker passes.
changes: living curve towers on 'far more strongly'
collapses on 'faded when the animal died'
scenes.words: because the dead ears missed something later measurements in living animals showed the membrane responding far more strongly to quiet sounds and far more sharply tuned than anything in b k sy's cadavers and that extra sensitivity faded when the animal died something in a living cochlea was adding energy

scenes.anchor: someone had predicted exactly this
scenes.visual: A 1948 typewritten-style paper card (our own typography, not a scan) titled with the idea, a hand-drawn amplifier symbol feeding energy into a damped wave; then dust settles over the card and a '30 years' counter runs.
text: the ear must contain an amplifier
scenes.words: someone had predicted exactly this in nineteen forty eight a young cambridge physicist thomas gold argued that the ear must contain an amplifier something actively pumping energy in to overcome the damping of the fluid hardly anyone took it up the idea was largely forgotten for about thirty years

scenes.anchor: to find gold's amplifier
scenes.visual: HERO 3 (3D). Inside the cochlear duct: one row of inner hair cells and three rows of outer hair cells on the membrane, each topped with stepped tufts of stereocilia (V/W shape for outer cells). Slow lateral dolly along the rows.
changes: inner row highlights on 'inner hair cells'
three outer rows highlight on 'three rows'
scenes.words: to find gold's amplifier look at the hair cells the cochlea has two kinds one row of inner hair cells about three and a half thousand of them and usually three rows of outer hair cells roughly three times as many

scenes.anchor: each is topped with a tuft
scenes.visual: Real scanning electron micrograph of stereocilia in their stepped rows (NIDCD, Bechara Kachar; public domain), framed as a FIG. card, slow push.
scenes.asset: NIDCD stereocilia SEM, cochlea, Yoshiyuki Kawashima (Wikimedia Commons, federal work, public domain)
scenes.words: each is topped with a tuft of tiny hairs called stereocilia

scenes.anchor: when the membrane moves the stereocilia bend
scenes.visual: One hair cell in 2D. The tuft tilts; tip channels open; small lime dots flow in; a lime pulse runs down to the nerve fibre.
changes: lime pulse down the nerve on 'hearing nerve'
scenes.words: when the membrane moves the stereocilia bend that opens tiny channels at their tips charged particles rush in and the cell makes an electrical signal for the hearing nerve

scenes.anchor: now here's the strange part
scenes.visual: Wiring diagram: nerve fibres (lime) fanning to the hair cells. Thick bundle to the single inner row; a few thin threads to the three outer rows. A 95 / 5 split bar.
changes: thick bundle to inner row on 'ninety-five percent'
thin threads to outer rows on 'five percent'
question mark on 'what are they for'
scenes.words: now here's the strange part about ninety five percent of the fibres in your hearing nerve carry signals from the inner hair cells only about five percent connect to the outer hair cells so three quarters of your hair cells barely talk to the brain what are they for

scenes.anchor: in nineteen eighty-five william brownell
scenes.visual: Lab-dish card: an isolated outer hair cell (tall cylinder) between two electrodes; the cell visibly shortens and lengthens with the polarity (violet glow marks the motor).
changes: cell isolated on 'took outer hair cells out'
text: Univ. of Florida · lab in Geneva
scenes.words: in nineteen eighty five william brownell found a big clue he was a hearing researcher from the university of florida working in a lab in geneva switzerland he and his colleagues took outer hair cells out of animal ears and applied a current the cells physically changed length shorter one way longer the other they're not just sensors they're motors

scenes.anchor: in two thousand researchers at northwestern
scenes.visual: Zoom into the cell wall: a lattice of prestin molecules (simple violet shapes) packed in the membrane, flexing together. A music score marking 'presto' appears beside the name.
scenes.words: in two thousand researchers at northwestern university found the protein that drives them they named it prestin after the musical marking presto fast

scenes.anchor: and fast they are
scenes.visual: Oscilloscope: the drive signal and the cell's length change tracking it at rising frequency; a ruler marks the top of human hearing and the cell keeps going past it.
changes: frequency sweeps up on 'tens of thousands'
passes the hearing limit on 'highest pitch'
text: tens of thousands of times a second
scenes.words: and fast they are in lab tests on isolated cells outer hair cells kept changing length in step with the signal tens of thousands of times a second faster than the highest pitch you can hear

scenes.anchor: by pushing on the membrane in time
scenes.visual: HERO 4 (3D, reuses HERO 3 set). The outer hair cells pump in sync with the passing wave; the membrane's peak grows taller and narrower where they push. A thin violet pulse overlay marks each push. Then 'whisper' (small wave) gets a big lift, 'shout' (big wave) barely changes.
scenes.words: by pushing on the membrane in time with the sound they boost the faintest vibrations roughly a hundredfold and sharpen the tuning they turn up whispers much more than shouts

scenes.anchor: the proof came from mice
scenes.visual: Two mouse outlines with audiogram-style bars: normal vs prestin-free. The prestin-free bar drops 40-60 dB while its hair-cell tufts still bend (shown small).
changes: bar drops on 'forty to sixty decibels'
tufts still bend on 'still sense motion'
scenes.words: the proof came from mice mice engineered without prestin lost that movement and became forty to sixty decibels less sensitive even though their hair cells could still sense motion

scenes.anchor: gold was right
scenes.visual: The microphone schematic from S08 returns and cracks apart; the amplifier symbol from S19 takes its place over the cochlea.
scenes.words: gold was right the ear isn't a microphone it has an amplifier built in

scenes.anchor: and amplifiers have a side effect
scenes.visual: Return to the probe-in-canal diagram from S02 (callback), now drawn with a 1978 lab label; clicks go in; after a delay a violet ring comes out; the scope shows the delayed violet wiggle with a 'few ms' bracket.
changes: violet ring out on 'came back out'
scenes.words: and amplifiers have a side effect in nineteen seventy eight david kemp a physicist working at a london ear hospital played clicks into people's ears and recorded what came back a few milliseconds later a faint sound came back out of the ear made inside the cochlea

scenes.anchor: it was there in every normal ear
scenes.visual: Two scope traces side by side: normal ear (violet echo present), cochlear deafness (flat).
scenes.words: it was there in every normal ear he tested and missing in ears with cochlear deafness

scenes.anchor: the same outer-hair-cell activity
scenes.visual: HERO 5 (3D, reuses HERO 2/4). The wave runs in, the outer hair cells pump, and a small reverse wave (violet overlay) runs back out toward the base; cut to the 2D path back through bones and eardrum to the probe microphone.
changes: reverse wave on 'sends a tiny wave back out'
path to eardrum on 'to the eardrum'
mic picks up on 'pick it up'
scenes.words: the same outer hair cell activity that boosts incoming sound sends a tiny wave back out through the middle ear to the eardrum where a sensitive microphone can pick it up

scenes.anchor: these are otoacoustic emissions
scenes.visual: The probe-in-canal diagram again (smaller, left), violet rings from inside the ear looping out to the probe; check mark for 'checks the ear, not the nerve'; 98-of-100 dot grid. No photo (Michael 2026-11-13).
changes: check and label on 'outer hair cells'
text: checks the ear, not the nerve
scenes.words: these are otoacoustic emissions and that's what the newborn test is listening for a clear response means the outer hair cells and the middle ear are working it's a check of the ear not the hearing nerve so when the nerve is the question babies get a different test that measures how the nerve and brainstem respond in twenty twenty about ninety eight out of every hundred babies born in the united states were screened

scenes.anchor: and many healthy ears go further
scenes.visual: The crowd of heads from S04 returns; the violet tone rings now pulse steadily; a spectrum display shows one or two thin steady peaks. Then the SIMULATION card: a waveform plays with the label held on screen the whole time.
changes: women/men note on 'more common in women'
text: more than half of people with normal hearing
SIMULATION · real tones are far too quiet to hear
scenes.words: and many healthy ears go further with no sound going in at all they give off faint steady tones spontaneous otoacoustic emissions more than half of people with normal hearing have at least one newborns included and they're more common in women than in men they're very quiet usually far too faint for you to notice here's a simulation of one turned up until you can hear it

scenes.anchor: an amplifier this good comes at a cost
scenes.visual: A decibel ladder (chalk): quiet room, conversation, 70 dB line ('unlikely to harm'), 85 dB line (marked), louder levels above with a shrinking 'safe time' bar.
changes: time bar shrinks on 'the less time it takes'
scenes.words: an amplifier this good comes at a cost long or repeated exposure to sound at or above eighty five decibels can damage hearing the louder the sound the less time it takes

scenes.anchor: and outer hair cells the amplifiers
scenes.visual: HERO 6 (3D, reuses HERO 3). The hair-cell rows; starting at the base end, outer-hair-cell tufts in the first row splay and go grey (muted), spreading along the high-pitch end. Inner row stays.
changes: first outer row greys on 'among the first'
loss spreads at the base on 'high pitches'
text: among the first cells noise destroys
scenes.words: and outer hair cells the amplifiers are among the first cells loud noise destroys high pitches usually go first the most hair cell loss shows up at the high frequency end the base of the cochlea

scenes.anchor: lose the outer hair cells
scenes.visual: The living vs dead curves from S18 return: the living curve falls to the broad, low one. Two close pitches that were separate peaks now blur into one.
scenes.words: lose the outer hair cells and you lose the amplifier in animal studies hearing became about fifty decibels less sensitive and the sharp tuning blurred quiet sounds vanish sounds close in pitch become harder to tell apart

scenes.anchor: and here's the hard part
scenes.visual: Side by side: mammal hair-cell row with gaps that stay empty; bird hair-cell row whose gaps refill (1988).
scenes.words: and here's the hard part in humans and in mammals generally lost hair cells don't grow back the damage is permanent birds are different in nineteen eighty eight two research teams showed that birds regrow their hair cells after noise damage we can't

scenes.anchor: for long days around loud sound
scenes.visual: The dB ladder returns with an 8-hour clock beside the 85 dB line. Quiet, factual, no alarm graphics.
scenes.words: for long days around loud sound the us workplace safety agency recommends a limit of eighty five decibels averaged over an eight hour shift

scenes.anchor: so the next time it's quiet
scenes.visual: HERO 7 (3D, reuses HERO 1). Pull back from the hair-cell rows out through the uncoiled membrane, which re-coils into the shell, which sits small inside the ear section; faint violet rings breathe out of it.
scenes.words: so the next time it's quiet really quiet remember what's going on inside your head a row of tiny motors pushing back against every sound you hear tens of thousands of times a second turning whispers up sharpening every note and quietly singing back

scenes.anchor: your ear was never a microphone
scenes.visual: The wordmark settles (as P1's closing); 'Next time' card.
scenes.words: your ear was never a microphone it was designed otherwise next time on designed otherwise
